topic: Research: Claude Code Async Workflows: Background Agents and Parallel Task Patterns (2026)

key_points: Official Claude Code docs frame parallel work as four different approaches: subagents, agent view, agent teams, and dynamic workflows.

Subagents are best for delegated side tasks inside one session, agent view is for dispatching and monitoring independent background sessions, teams are for coordinated multi-session work, and dynamic workflows are script-driven fan-out with cross-checking.
Worktrees are the isolation mechanism for parallel sessions so multiple agents do not edit the same checkout.
Subagents are specialized AI assistants with their own context window, custom system prompt, tool access, and permissions.
The docs emphasize context management: use subagents when research, logs, or file reads would pollute the main conversation.
Important sections for the article include foreground vs background execution, parallel research, chained subagents, nested subagents, resume behavior, and auto-compaction.
Anthropic positions subagents, hooks, and background tasks as a combined autonomy upgrade for larger refactors and feature exploration.
Subagents enable parallel development such as one worker building an API while the main agent builds a frontend.
Hooks and background tasks matter because async work is only useful when test, lint, and long-running process feedback can continue without blocking the main loop.
Competitor article targets the exact keyword cluster and focuses on the practical Ctrl+B workflow for moving a running subagent into the background.
Covers checking background agents with /tasks, monitoring token usage and progress, and choosing which jobs belong in the background.
Useful but vendor-adjacent angle: pushes packaged orchestration kits, so our article can differentiate with a more neutral decision framework and governance guidance.
CloudZero focuses on cost and operational planning for Claude Code agents rather than only the mechanics of running them.
Highlights that parallelism multiplies token consumption because each background session draws from the same plan or API budget.
Good competitor gap: cost math, plan limits, and governance should be treated as first-class parts of async workflow design.

stats.fact: Claude Code docs now distinguish four parallel-work modes: subagents, agent view, agent teams, and dynamic workflows, each intended for a different coordination pattern.

Anthropic says worktrees give each parallel session a separate git checkout; agent view automatically moves dispatched sessions into their own worktrees, and spawned subagents can get isolated worktrees too.

Anthropic's cost docs estimate Claude Code averages about $13 per developer per active day and $150-$250 per developer per month across enterprise deployments, with 90% of users below $30 per active day.
Google's 2025 DORA coverage says AI adoption among software development professionals reached 90%, up 14% year over year, with a median of two hours per day spent working with AI.

Microsoft reported on June 5, 2026 that Anthropic mitigated a Claude Code GitHub Action secret exposure issue in Claude Code 2.1.128 by blocking access to sensitive /proc files, underscoring that async CI/CD agents need strict secret boundaries.
The Claude Code GitHub Action supports issue assignments, @claude mentions, explicit automation prompts, progress tracking, structured outputs, and running on the user's own GitHub runner.

angles: Async is not one feature: explain the decision tree between backgrounding a subagent, opening agent view, using agent teams, or scripting a dynamic workflow.
The real throughput gain comes from dependency design: parallelize independent research, audits, test generation, migrations, and review passes, but keep dependent edits sequential.
Worktree isolation is the difference between useful parallelism and merge-conflict chaos; every serious pattern should name its file ownership and integration step.
Cost and quota become workflow constraints once agents run in parallel; five agents can mean five concurrent token streams, not one smarter stream.
Security needs a separate section for CI/CD and GitHub Actions because background agents may process untrusted issue, PR, and comment text while secrets are present.
A good 2026 guide should include operating rituals: assign narrow scopes, require artifacts, cross-check results, merge deliberately, and kill or pause background work that loses its objective.
Differentiate from how-to-only competitors by giving readers a practical pattern catalog and anti-patterns for async Claude Code work.
